name: FSE-ready practice and billing tool for small private clinics and doctors (CNSS homologation, CNOPS to CNSS 2027)
buyer: Solo doctors, small specialist cabinets and small clinics billing AMO
trigger: CNSS FSE and software homologation
reason: The CNSS FSE is real, but no source I found shows it is mandatory per practitioner. A 2026 rollout is reported, but I found no article dated later than May 2026, so the October 2026 status is unknown. The CNSS offers a free FSE portal to doctors, so the core job is covered by the state. Practitioners can also transmit from interoperable software. Homologation is under way, with Nabady in the final test stage in May 2026. TabibDoc, Docdialy and Pratisoft already sell practice software, so the field is crowded. Private doctors' unions resist the FSE and want subsidies, which weakens willingness to pay. The market is about 15,399 private consultation cabinets (carte sanitaire 2025, via Telquel). No penalty was found. Not reached: the official list of homologated software and the CNSS site.

name: AML Procedures and UTRFNET Onboarding for Insurance Agents and Small Brokers (ACAPS)
buyer: Insurance agencies and small brokerages (agents of insurers and courtiers)
trigger: ACAPS AML circular and UTRFNET suspicion reporting
reason: The duty is real. ACAPS circular AS/02/19, amended by AS/03/21, sets AML/CFT due diligence for insurers and intermediaries. ACAPS inspections ran from Q1 2021 to Q1 2022. They found 87% of inspected intermediaries without UTRFNET (now ANRFNET) access, and 37% without formal procedures. None had filed a suspicious transaction report. Sanctions were proposed against 6 intermediaries. The market is about 2,460 firms (603 brokers and 1,859 agents as of March 2026, per Challenge.ma). The duty is ad hoc: KYC, procedures and suspicion reports, with no periodic filing. Competitor search was shallow and found no dedicated tool, but the product would mostly be a policy template plus KYC checklist. Insurers largely carry agents' compliance, and ACAPS gives free guides. The market is small, the filing is rare and willingness to pay is low. I did not read the circular text itself.

name: Public-contract Labour Compliance Pack for guarding, cleaning and catering contractors
buyer: Small guarding (law 27-06), cleaning and catering contractors on public contracts, and the public bodies that hire them
trigger: Labour inspection of public-contract contractors and SMIG revisions
reason: Labour inspection of public-contract guarding, cleaning and catering firms is real: about 25,000 visits and 335,000 observations in 2025, with 85,000 on wage non-conformity (SNRT, minister's statement of 27 Apr 2026). That is enforcement, not a recurring filing to an authority. I found no specific recurring report beyond ordinary CNSS declarations and SMIG pay compliance, which is generic payroll and out of scope. I found no dedicated competitor, but payroll vendors such as Damancom and SIMPL are adjacent. The 27-06 prior declaration of hires appears in a secondary summary only, with no current official text. The only market figure is about 400 guarding firms in 2013 (Medias24), with 15 large firms holding 45% of the market. There is no count for cleaning or catering. The buyer group is fragmented and low-margin. This is a weak fit as a product.

name: Private School Compliance Calendar (authorisation display, textbook sample submission, family contract)
buyer: Small private schools, nurseries and tutoring centres
trigger: Annual textbook declaration and family contract duties for private schools
reason: Duty is real but the claim is a bundle of mostly one-off or diffuse items, not a clean recurring workflow. Law 06.00 requires prior academy authorisation and gives the academy pedagogic and administrative control. A school-family contract was applied by circular from 2023-24. In May 2025 the minister said an annual written contract would become mandatory, but binding force depends on law 59.21. I found no confirmation that law 59.21 was adopted. July 2026 coverage (Telquel) only restates the ban on forcing families to buy textbooks. I did not find a "textbook sample submission" duty. Competition: generic school-management software exists (e.g. OpenEduCat with MAD billing). Market: 6,922 private schools in 2019-20 (Conseil de la concurrence via Le360), probably more now, but most are not tiny. Whether Massar entry is mandatory for private schools was not found. Willingness to pay is likely low and the duty is thin.

name: Technical Inspection Centre Operations (NARSA network audit and 240 new centres)
buyer: Owners and operators of vehicle inspection centres and network operators
trigger: NARSA 2025-2028 plan for 240 new centres (439 existing); network audit tender Nov 2024; centres belong to an approved network and aim for ISO 17020; stricter 2026 checks reported by autoactu (no official text cited).
reason: The sector is real. Press reports (aujourdhui.ma, La Vie Eco, wandaloo) say 4 networks run 439 centres, and NARSA has tendered 240 new ones (201 light-vehicle, 39 heavy-vehicle) under the 2025-2028 plan. A Nov 2024 network-audit tender and an ISO 17020 target are also reported. But this is not a recurring small-business filing duty. It is a licensed operator regime, and the buyer is a few networks that likely tie software to their own systems or to NARSA. I found no vendor, no NARSA data-exchange standard and no official text for the "2026 checks". The 2016 tender filled only 83 of 192 slots, which suggests few buyers. The buyer pool is tiny, and the idea overlaps K02.

name: MoFFA Mortuary and Funeral Home Licensing Compliance Desk
buyer: Private mortuaries and funeral homes (at least 232 identified mortuaries, none licensed as of 2025; funeral homes count unknown)
trigger: Health Institutions and Facilities Act 2011 (Act 829) created MoFFA. Licensing of all facilities is being rolled out with practical licensure exams for workers, inspections and closures in 2025-26 (Feb 2026 closures, 24 Aug 2026 Volta inspections, district monitoring officers announced). Standards include management structure, ownership, financial capacity, infection control, security, a backup generator and a one-week water tank.
duty: Health Institutions and Facilities Act 2011 (Act 829): MoFFA licenses facilities that store, transport or dispose of human remains. Under s.55, operating unlicensed or practising unregistered is an offence, punished by a fine or temporary or permanent closure. Enforcement is active: an Oct 2025 one-week ultimatum, Eastern Region closures, a 10-day notice in Ashanti, Volta inspections in Aug 2026 and district officers from Aug 2026. Renewal frequency, fees and required registers were not found (not_reached).
market: At least 232 mortuaries (Graphic, Sep 2023), none licensed then. MoFFA records: 17 in 2022, 125 in 2023. Most are attached to hospitals (public, mission or CHAG). A GCPS journal paper says virtually all storage facilities are in hospitals and funeral homes are few. Small private buyers likely number well under 200.
competitor: MortemCare is Ghana-based cloud mortuary/funeral home software covering intake, deceased records and billing, with Free, $199/mo and $499/mo tiers (per PricingSaaS). No MoFFA licensing features were seen. Foreign tools: Dedalus Mortuary MIS (hospital), SafetyCulture checklists, Osiris, Gather, Passare. No MoFFA online portal was found. A 2023 Graphic report says MoFFA plans a digital system where operators key in information in real time.
reason: The duty is real: Act 829 has MoFFA license mortuaries, and Section 55 punishes unlicensed operation with a fine or closure. Enforcement is live, with an Oct 2025 one-week ultimatum, closures, 2026 inspections and district officers. No MoFFA-specific compliance tool or online portal was found. The fit is weak, though. Most of the work is physical (generator, water tank, sanitation, PPE) and a one-off licence plus worker exam. Renewal frequency and record-reporting rules are unknown. Most mortuaries sit in public or mission hospitals rather than small private firms. MortemCare, a Ghana-based cloud mortuary system (free/$199/$499 a month), already covers intake and deceased records. MoFFA has also talked of a planned digital system where operators key in data.

name: Private Employment Agency Licence and Quarterly Returns Desk
buyer: Licensed private employment and recruitment agencies (limited companies only; count unverified)
trigger: Labour Act 2003 s.7 and Labour Regulations L.I. 1833 (2007): licence renewal 2 months before expiry (2 years), quarterly report to the Chief Labour Officer within 14 days of quarter end, otherwise the Minister revokes the licence. Government statements in 2023 and later on unlicensed agencies suggest tighter enforcement.
duty: Licence renewal every 2 years (apply 2 months before expiry) plus quarterly reports to Chief Labour Officer within 14 days of quarter end; licence revoked/withdrawn for non-compliance
market: Roughly 19 to 200 licensed agencies (conflicting 2014/2015 figures); current count unverified
competitor: none found specific to Ghana (generic HR/recruitment tools not checked)
reason: The duty is real. LI 1833 and Labour Act 651 require corporate private employment agencies to renew their licence 2 months before expiry (24-month term) and file quarterly reports within 14 days of quarter end. Revocation or withdrawal of the licence is the penalty. I found no Ghana-specific software or online portal doing this. The market is tiny: counts conflict (about 200 licensed in 2014, with 96 in good standing; 19 in 2015). Only a few dozen to a couple hundred buyers, a 2-year renewal cycle, and low fees (GH¢500-1,000) give weak willingness to pay. I could not confirm the current form or fee schedule, or whether filing is online. Revoked in the sense of a niche: low score.

name: Annual Returns and Beneficial-Ownership Filing Service for Churches, NGOs and Associations
buyer: Churches, charities, associations, clubs, unions and NGOs incorporated as companies limited by guarantee
trigger: Companies Act 2019 (Act 992) s.126: annual return at least once a year plus financial statements and beneficial ownership information; penalty raised to GHS 1,000 plus GHS 350 per month from 1 May 2024; deadline extended to 30 Sep 2024 once; 2,812 churches, clubs, unions and associations were blacklisted for non-filing in 2023.
duty: Companies Act 2019 (Act 992) s.126(1): every company, including companies limited by guarantee (churches, NGOs, clubs, associations), must file an annual return once a year, first within 18 months of incorporation. The return must include audited financial statements and beneficial-ownership (BO) data (BO data required since 31 Mar 2021). ORC set 30 Apr 2026 as the deadline for FY2025 and later extended it to 30 Jun 2026, so the duty is in force and recurring. Penalties: GHS 1,000 plus GHS 350 per month from May 2024. The 2026 release instead gives tiers of GHS 1,000 for 1-4 years in default and GHS 2,000 for 5+ years, and these two schedules do not clearly reconcile. Strike-off is possible. A separate GHS 500 fine for not filing BO data has been enforced since 12 Jan 2026, with up to 250 penalty units or 2 years in prison for false declarations.
market: ORC reported only 19,074 companies limited by guarantee in good standing in 2023, plus an unknown number in default. In 2023 ORC blacklisted 2,812 churches, clubs, unions and associations. As of Feb 2023, only 25.8% of 287,189 registered companies had disclosed BO data. I found no current official count of LBGs; the realistic base is roughly 20,000-40,000 LBGs.
killer: No software kills it. In practice, auditors and company secretaries already file the return along with the statutory audit, and the audited financial statements the return requires can only come from a chartered accountant (ORC Online Renewals page; secretarial firms listed on businessghana.com).
reason: The duty is real, annual and enforced, with penalties, strike-offs and new BO fines in 2026. No dedicated software or packaged service for non-profits turned up, so this counts as confirmed. The core burden, though, is the audited financial statements, which only licensed auditors can produce, and accountants and company secretaries already bundle the filing with the audit. Filing still looks paper or office based, which helps a done-for-you service but makes a pure-software MVP harder. The buyer pool is small (about 19k LBGs in good standing) and price-sensitive, since churches and small NGOs pay small fees, and the government filing fee is only about GHS 90. A service is best sold through church denominations or NGO networks, or as a BO plus annual-return reminder and preparation tool for accountants.
challenge_reason: I found no dedicated product, so this is not refuted. But the core job is weak for software. The duty is real and enforced: the 2026 deadline was 30 June, with no extension, flat penalties of GHS 1,000 to 2,000, and strike-offs (an earlier sweep removed 978 companies limited by guarantee). Most of the cost and effort is the audited financial statements that must be attached, and only a chartered accountant can produce those. That makes auditors and company secretaries the natural incumbent, bundling this with the audit. The ORC form itself is simple and costs GHS 90-100. Non-profits also report separately to the NPO Secretariat. Willingness to pay looks low and the incorporated non-profit market is small. I could not confirm whether ORC e-filing exists.

name: Water Drilling Licence, Notice and Well-Record Filing for Borehole Drillers
buyer: Licensed water drilling companies (about 100 to 200 per WRC statements, count unverified) and well owners who must register boreholes
trigger: Drilling Licence and Groundwater Development Regulations L.I. 1827 (2006): licence, renewal 30 days before expiry, notice of intention to construct a well, well records submission, WRC arrests and fines of GHS 60,000 for unlicensed drillers; public tenders check the licence.
reason: Duty is real: L.I. 1827 (2006) requires a WRC drilling licence (renewal at least 30 days before expiry), with fines up to 200 penalty units and/or 12 months (unlicensed), 250 penalty units/2 years (breach of conditions); WRC has fined firms GHS 60,000. No driller software or online WRC system found, though the search was not exhaustive. Market is tiny: about 200 licensed firms, with licence renewal annual and well-record filing per job. Buyers are small, low-tech, and have low willingness to pay. Well-owner registration is a weak, unenforced demand. Notice and well-record provisions were not read in full (PDF not fetched). Too small for a standalone product.

name: Pesticide and Fertiliser Retailer Licence and Attendant Certification Desk
buyer: Agro-chemical retail shops, warehouses and commercial pest controllers licensed by EPA; fertiliser retailers under PPRSD (about 700 rural fertiliser retailers cited)
trigger: Act 528 (EPA licence for importers, distributors, warehouses, retailers, pest controllers; one source lists the Act as repealed, unconfirmed) and Plants and Fertilizer Act 2010 (Act 803); EPA and police operations against dealers with expired licences.
duty: EPA dealer, premises and pest controller licence renewal (annual) with an annual pesticide report; PPRSD registration of fertiliser dealers under Act 803. The Act 528 and 1124 basis and current fees are unconfirmed.
market: No national count found; 2011 Eastern Region sample was 505 shops; a donor target of 2,200 dealers to train; PPRSD cited about 700 rural fertiliser retailers.
competitor: None found
reason: The duty is real. The EPA licenses agro-chemical dealers (retailers, distributors, importers, warehouses, pest controllers), with annual premises licence renewal and annual pesticide reports. PPRSD registers fertiliser dealers under Act 803. Enforcement is real: closures and prosecution threats in 2011 and 2019, and in 2011 only 15 of 505 Eastern Region shops held permits. I could not confirm the current Act 528 or Act 1124 legal basis, current fees, or the renewal cycle. Wiki sources conflict on both validity period and processing time. The 2011 compliance figures show low compliance and weak buyer willingness to pay. I found no national count of licensed dealers; the sources give only a donor target of 2,200 agro-input dealers to train. I found no competing software, but I also found no evidence of demand. Buyers are informal rural shops with low digital maturity. The recurring filing is one annual renewal plus an annual report, which is thin.

name: Commercial Vehicle Roadworthy and Insurance Renewal Reminders for Taxi and Trotro Owners
buyer: Taxi, trotro and ride-hail owners
trigger: L.I. 2180 DVLA roadworthy certificate; DVLA sanctioned 1,251 vehicles in Accra in one sweep; ride-hail cars said to renew twice a year (2019 statement).
duty: L.I. 2180 (Road Traffic Regulations 2012) roadworthy certificate; L.I. 2220 delinquency charges; compulsory motor insurance. Interval for commercial vehicles unconfirmed, with six-monthly cited only in 2018.
market: Not quantified (no register or statistic checked); a large informal taxi and trotro base is implied
competitor: DVLA SMS expiry alerts (announced January 2026); NIC *920*57# insurance check; no fleet reminder app found
reason: The duty is real. L.I. 2180 requires physical roadworthy inspection and certification. DVLA enforces it and charges delinquency fees under L.I. 2220 for expired certificates. Courts fine taxi drivers for lapsed roadworthy and insurance. The twice-yearly interval comes only from a 2018 DVLA statement about ride-hail cars. I could not confirm a current interval for taxis or trotros. DVLA announced SMS renewal reminders in January 2026, and rollout is unconfirmed. NIC offers *920*57# insurance checks. I found no fleet-owner reminder app. The weak points are the buyer and the pitch. Owners are informal and low-margin, and a reminder tool is generic and nearly free to replicate, while DVLA's own SMS undercuts it. Willingness to pay is low. This is adjacent to K04 and K15 (rejected), not a new buyer group. No revival evidence.

name: C01 Fire-equipment tagging and permit desk for GNFS-licensed Fire Protection Contractors and property managers (AFCAS)
buyer: Licensed fire protection contractors and extinguisher servicers (small firms), plus property managers and small commercial premises owners
trigger: Fire Precaution (Premises) Regulations 2003 (L.I. 1724) as amended by L.I. 2249: fire permit and certificate for all premises, regs 11-12 tag all alarms/extinguishers with GNFS-AFCAS QR code; existing equipment must be tagged within six months of the 28 Aug 2026 announcement (about end Feb 2027); procurement must use licensed contractors
duty: Real and in force. L.I. 1724 (2003), as amended by L.I. 2249 (2016), requires a fire certificate for all non-domestic premises (shops, offices, hotels, factories, fuel stations and so on). The penalty is up to 250 penalty units and/or 12 months in prison, and GNFS does close premises. Regs 11-12 require GNFS tags on alarms and extinguishers. The AFCAS rollout (Aug-Sep 2026) gives owners of existing equipment six months to get it tagged by GNFS-authorised inspectors. Every fire protection contractor must register on AFCAS (registration opened 3 Aug), in classes A-E (A = equipment servicing, E = import), and each class must be renewed. The certificate validity period, the renewal cycle and the fees were not confirmed.
market: No count of licensed contractors was found. AFCAS publishes a directory but no total, and I found no trade association. Contractors are probably in the low hundreds nationally. The premises carrying the certificate duty run to tens or hundreds of thousands, but GNFS says over 70% of properties have no valid certificate, which points to weak compliance and low willingness to pay.
competitor: AFCAS (afcas.gnfs.gov.gh) is the free state portal, and it already does the core job. It handles permit and certificate applications and issues certificates with QR codes. It sends automated renewal reminders 90, 60 and 30 days before expiry. Its Fire Equipment Tagging and Tracking System holds each item's maintenance history and sends automatic alerts when servicing or replacement is due. Its Provider Portal lets contractors manage their profile, submit drawings and proposal reports, and register and tag equipment. What is left is generic field-service or job management for contractors, which international products such as InspectNTrack, Inspect Point, FlameTask and Ecesis already cover. I found no Ghana-specific vendor.
reason: The duty is real and has a near-term tagging deadline (about Feb-Mar 2027). But the free AFCAS portal already handles the core of the claimed product: permit and certificate applications, QR certificates, renewal reminders at 90/60/30 days, an equipment tagging registry with servicing alerts, and a provider portal where contractors register and tag equipment. That leaves contractor job and field-service management, which is generic software that existing international tools already offer. The buyer pool of licensed contractors is likely small, and compliance among premises owners is weak. Some done-for-you consulting demand might appear around the tagging deadline, but it does not hold up as a defensible software product.

name: C02 NACOC registration and licence-renewal file for pharmacies, chemical sellers and labs handling precursors/psychotropics
buyer: Retail and wholesale pharmacies, licensed chemical sellers, private labs, small importers, educational/industrial users of controlled equipment
trigger: Narcotics Control Commission Act 2020 (Act 1019): all persons dealing in precursor chemicals, psychotropic substances and controlled equipment must register or regularise by 31 Jul 2026 and renew licences before expiry; sanctions administrative, civil or criminal
duty: Narcotics Control Commission Act 2020 (Act 1019): register/licence with NACOC before operating; notice of 7 Jul 2026 set a 31 Jul 2026 deadline (passed); renew licences when due (cycle unspecified); sanctions administrative/civil/criminal. Pharmacies named in Graphic headline but not in notice body (covers retail/wholesale/labs/educational/industrial users). Post-registration records/returns not_reached.
market: Not found. Pharmacy Council publishes annual gazette of licensed pharmacies and OTCMS (ex-licensed chemical sellers), only on written request to the Registrar. Regional study: 208 OTCMS in Upper East region alone, suggesting national pharmacies+OTCMS are in the many thousands, but how many handle NACOC-scheduled substances is unknown.
competitor: No software or consultancy found doing NACOC registration or controlled-substance registers in Ghana. No NACOC online portal found; notice says contact the Commission directly. Pharmacy POS vendors (e.g., Frevie Desk) don't show NACOC features. Not a kill, but an absent portal limits automation.
reason: Duty confirmed: NACOC's 7 July 2026 notice under Act 1019 (in force) required everyone handling precursors, psychotropics or controlled equipment to register by 31 Jul 2026, with administrative, civil or criminal sanctions. That deadline passed over two months ago and no extension was found, so the one-off rush is over. The only recurring part is renewing licences 'when due'; frequency, fees, required records and returns, and any NACOC portal are all unknown. No competitor found, but the core job looks like occasional paperwork, not a workflow. No count of registrants found: the Pharmacy Council's facility gazette is only given out on written request. Low frequency, buyers bunched among pharmacies; better bundled into pharmacy compliance software than sold alone.

name: C03 Data-protection registration, renewal and compliance file for small data controllers (clinics, schools, churches, SMEs)
buyer: Small organisations processing personal data: private clinics, schools, churches, agents, lenders, retailers with customer lists
trigger: Data Protection Act 2012 (Act 843): register within 20 days of starting business (s.97), renew (3 months before expiry per DPC manual; 2-year cycle per 2023 guide); DPC spot checks and prosecution threat began 5 Oct 2026; arrears back to 2012 possible
duty: Real and in force. The Data Protection Act 2012 (Act 843) requires every data controller and processor to register with the DPC before processing personal data (s.46ff). The DPC registration manual says to apply for renewal 3 months before expiry; failing to renew means removal from the register. Sources disagree on the cycle: 2 years per a vendor summary, 3 years per an unofficial wiki. Penalty for unregistered processing is up to 250 penalty units or 2 years in prison, but only a vendor summary (ConsentStack) says so; I did not check it against the Act. GNA (4 Oct 2026) confirms spot checks started 5 Oct 2026, covering registration and other duties, with prosecution where necessary. There is a risk the rules change: a draft new Data Protection Bill went to consultation in Oct 2025 and would license data protection service providers. The DPC site now points to a new domain, dpc.gov.gh.
market: Not reached. The Minister reported new registered controllers up 98.4% and regulatory activity up 51.5% in H1 2026, but gave no totals. The duty covers practically every formal business that keeps customer or staff data, which is in the hundreds of thousands. An older 2015 report says only about 20k of 60k data-collection businesses were certified. I found no current count of DPC registrants.
competitor: The core filing job is already done by the DPC's free online registration and renewal portal (RegSys) and its free online self-assessment tool. DPO-as-a-service and privacy audits are sold by GIT Plus Limited, law firms such as B&P Associates, and DPC-accredited training providers. Generic Act 843 compliance SaaS also exists (ConsentStack). I found no SME-focused app for renewal tracking or the compliance file, but the gap is thin: small-business fees are only about GH¢120–156, so most of the value is reminders and paperwork.
reason: The duty is real and broad, and enforcement started on 5 Oct 2026, which creates a short window of urgency. The core job, registering and renewing, is done free on the DPC's own portal. Small-business fees are only about GH¢120–156 every 2–3 years, so willingness to pay for software is low. The recurring part, renewal plus gap-analysis reports at renewal, adds some value. But consultants, law firms and accredited providers already sell DPO and compliance help to buyers who care. The pending Data Protection Bill may require service providers to be licensed, which adds regulatory risk. Best case is a cheap reminder and template add-on sold through accountants or associations, not a standalone business.
sources: https://gna.org.gh/2026/10/dpc-begins-checks-on-data-protection-compliance-2/ ; https://dataprotection.org.gh/registration/ ; https://dataprotection.org.gh/help-faqs/ (fee tiers seen in search snippet; page now redirects to dpc.gov.gh) ; https://dataprotection.org.gh/compliance/ ; https://www.myjoyonline.com/data-protection-commission-records-sharp-rise-in-regulatory-activity-sam-george/ ; https://www.consentstack.io/regulations/gh-act843 ; https://www.ghanaweb.com/org/GIT-Plus-Limited-1000214 ; https://digitalpolicyalert.org/event/34522-ministry-of-communication-digital-technology-and-innovations-opened-consultation-on-data-protection-act-2025-including-operational-license-requirements ; https://ghalii.org/akn/gh/act/2012/843

name: C04 Tourism-levy and GTA licence desk for guest houses, hostels and short-term-rental hosts
buyer: Guest houses, hostels, serviced apartments, Airbnb-type hosts (small and family-run)
trigger: Tourism Act 817 and L.I. 2185 licence; 1 percent Tourism Levy collected from guests with prescribed invoice, monthly return and remittance within a month; GTA may assess by estimate if records unreliable; short-term rental registration via GTA single window since Nov 2024 (host TIN or Ghana Card, business certificate); closures in 2026 for unlicensed or non-paying facilities
duty: The Tourism Act 2011 (Act 817) and its LIs (2238, 2239, 2393, 2389) are in force. The 1% Tourism Levy is charged on guests' bills at hotels, guest houses, lodges and hostels and remitted monthly. GTA enforces it with closures, for example 203 illegal facilities flagged in Ashanti in 2025 and earlier closures of levy defaulters. Short-term rentals need a provisional licence through the GTA single window, renewed every six months, under a transitional regime that started in Dec 2024. Draft 2026 regulations went to stakeholder consultation in July 2026.
market: MoTAC reports about 5,424 licensed accommodation establishments in 2025 (up from 5,210 in 2024) and 7,109 licensed tourism enterprises in total. There are roughly 4,000 to 5,000 Airbnb listings, mostly in Accra, and many are not registered.
competitor: The GTA's own Ghana Tourism Information System (GTIS) is free and live since 19 May 2026. It covers online registration and licensing, automatic levy calculation, digital payment of levies and audit charges, return filing, guest log data and public licence verification. E-licensing and a customer service register come in the next phase. Hotel PMS vendors (for example DJUBO) cover billing. The claim's premise that levy filing isn't digitised is out of date.
reason: The duty is real. Under Act 817, every licensed accommodation facility must collect the 1% Tourism Levy and remit it to the GTA, and facilities that are unlicensed or don't pay have been shut down. Since late 2024, short-term rental hosts also need a provisional GTA licence that is renewed every six months. The core job, though, is now covered by a free state system. GTA's GTIS went live on 19 May 2026. It handles registration and licensing, works out the levy automatically, takes levy and audit payments online, accepts filed returns, collects guest logs, and lets the public check a facility's licence. The only gaps are an electronic licensing phase that is still to come and a possible done-for-you service for informal Airbnb hosts. That is a thin service niche for about 5,400 accommodation facilities. Hotel PMS vendors such as DJUBO can add GTIS exports themselves.

name: C05 TCDA aggregator/trader licence, export-permit and conveyance-certificate desk for cashew, shea and rubber traders
buyer: About 1,600 registered aggregators, traders and importers of tree-crop produce plus small exporters of unprocessed cashew, shea and rubber
trigger: Tree Crops Development Authority Act 2019 (Act 1010) and L.I. 2471: operational licence, written export authorisation since 2 May 2025 (reg. 50), proof of levy payment before PPRSD phytosanitary certificate, statutory minimum farm-gate price (cashew GHS 12/kg), digital Conveyance Certificate System for trucks, fronting is criminal
duty: Act 1010 (2019) and L.I. 2471 (Tree Crops Regulations 2023) are in force. Aggregators, traders, processors and exporters need a TCDA operational licence, renewed each season; the 2025/26 cashew renewal was due 15 Jan 2026, with expected export volumes and levies due by the same date. Since 2 May 2025, reg. 50 requires written TCDA authorisation before exporting unprocessed cashew, shea or rubber, and PPRSD issues no phytosanitary certificate without proof the TCDA levy is paid. Since March 2026 the Conveyance Certificate System has applied nationwide to six crops, with Forestry Commission enforcement under an MoU. Shea levies are GHS1 per bag of nuts and GHS500 or GHS1,000 per truck of butter. Penalties: trading without a licence, buying below the floor price and fronting can bring arrest and prosecution. TCDA stepped up enforcement in September 2026. No fine amounts are published.
market: A GNA report (undated) says TCDA had registered about 1,600 aggregators, traders and importers. Exporters of unprocessed cashew and shea probably number only in the low hundreds. Most aggregators are rural Ghanaian small traders (foreigners are barred from aggregating) with limited digital literacy.
competitor: No third-party tool found that handles licence, export-permit, levy or conveyance paperwork. TraceX, Kolonell and a cashew union app do farm and sack traceability and buying-station payments, not this paperwork. TCDA issues conveyance certificates itself, at zonal offices and checkpoints at sourcing points, and describes its own digital licensing and traceability regime. No public portal or API was found, so there is little for third-party software to plug into.
reason: The duty is real, recurring and enforced: seasonal licences, a permit per export, levy proof before the phytosanitary certificate, and a certificate for each truck. No private paperwork tool exists. But the state issues every document itself, at its offices and checkpoints, and runs its own digital system, so software mostly helps with reminders and filing, not the core issuance. About 1,600 rural, low-margin, cash-based aggregators are unlikely to pay for SaaS. Exporters are fewer and already use clearing agents who do this paperwork. Without a public portal or API, an MVP could only offer reminders, document storage and levy tracking. A done-for-you desk run as a freight-agent add-on is the more plausible format, and it is service-heavy.

name: C12 Cylinder Recirculation Model outlet and exchange-point register for LPG distributors
buyer: LPG retail outlets converting into cylinder distribution points (510 high-risk outlets), LPG marketing companies, bottling plants
trigger: NPA Cylinder Recirculation Model full roll-out in 2026; consumers register at exchange points with Ghana Card; cylinders tracked; bottling plants licensed incrementally
duty: No confirmed duty. The NPA Cylinder Recirculation Model is a policy with licensing of bottling plants and exchange points. No 2026 instrument requiring outlets to keep a register or use tracking software was found.
market: Not quantified. The claim cites 510 high-risk LPG outlets, plus a handful of bottling plants and marketing companies. No register count was verified.
competitor: Polygon (Beijing) Energy Technology with Xpress Gas (LPG IoT/RFID cylinder tracking SaaS); in-house tracking by LPG marketing companies
reason: The CRM policy is real. In Feb 2026 the NPA said full roll-out would come in 2026, with Ghana Card registration at exchange points. I found no 2026 NPA circular, gazetted rule or directive that requires any outlet or exchange-point register or tracking software. So the duty on small businesses is unproven. Timelines have slipped repeatedly since 2023. Competition is emerging: Xpress Gas and Polygon announced RFID/QR cylinder-tracking SaaS in Aug 2026. Likely buyers are large marketing companies and bottling plants, which run their own tracking. Small outlets are not clearly obliged to file anything. No market count was found. The idea is weak on mandate, buyer and timing.

name: C16 Environmental permit and quarterly monitoring-return file for small regulated enterprises
buyer: Small regulated undertakings (quarries, plants, farms, workshops) holding or needing EPA permits
trigger: Environmental Protection Act 2025 (Act 1124) and L.I. 2504; nationwide permit regularisation drive Jan 2026; quarterly monitoring returns are a permit condition
duty: Real and in force, with caveats. Under the Environmental Protection Act, 2025 (Act 1124) and L.I. 2504, it is an offence to operate without an EPA permit, on an expired permit, or in breach of permit conditions. The EPA's 8 Jan 2026 notice set no deadline and warned of administrative penalties, fines, closure or prosecution. Permits are renewable, and one regional report says every 18 months. The older LI 1652 also requires an annual environmental report. Quarterly monitoring returns are a condition of some individual permits, not a general rule: the Sept 2026 Empire Cement shutdown cited Condition 9.1, quarterly air and noise returns. Sources disagree on whether returns are monthly or quarterly, and the evidence comes mainly from heavy industry, not small firms. I could not confirm the text of L.I. 2504 or its reporting clauses.
market: More than 33,370 applications have gone through the EPA's digital system, according to the EPA CEO. A cBrain vendor case study gives about 15,000 permits a year. The sectors covered are broad: fuel stations, hotels, bars and restaurants, clinics and labs, schools, places of worship, block makers, poultry and piggery farms, quarries and sand winning. How many of these firms actually have quarterly-return conditions is unknown, probably a small subset of industrial sites.
reason: The duty is real, recently tightened (Act 1124, the Jan 2026 enforcement drive) and carries penalties up to closure, and I found no SME software for it. But the core of the job is lab or field monitoring and certified-consultant work, not paperwork. Quarterly returns seem to apply mainly to larger industrial permits. Act 1124 s.31 limits environmental services to certified practitioners. Small hotels, fuel stations and churches mostly need permit renewal reminders and help with the application, which is low frequency and done in person at EPA offices. Willingness to pay for software is weak, so distribution would likely have to go through consultants. A renewal tracker plus a consultant marketplace is a thin MVP. I am keeping the score at 3.

name: C18 COCOBOD Licensed Buying Company purchase and no-credit compliance records
buyer: Indigenous Licensed Buying Companies (LICOBAG/COCOAMAG members)
trigger: COCOBOD ban on buying cocoa from farmers on credit (Aug 2026), licence revocation threat; Ghana Cocoa Board Bill passed 30 Jul 2026; domestic cocoa-bond financing from 2026/27 season
duty: Ban on LBCs buying cocoa from farmers on credit (Aug 2026 directive); repeat breach means licence revocation. No recurring record or reporting filing found.
market: Not found; LBC count not located (a small number of firms)
competitor: COCOBOD Cocoa Purchase App and LBC Depot App (Ghana Cocoa Traceability System)
reason: The claim is a prohibition, not a recurring compliance workflow. COCOBOD banned credit purchases in Aug 2026. Repeat breaches risk licence revocation, and no licences have been withdrawn. Reports mention no filings, records or reporting format. COCOBOD already runs the Cocoa Purchase App and LBC Depot App (Ghana Cocoa Traceability System). Roughly 900 clerks were trained on them in Dec 2023, and they record purchases and enable digital farmer payments. The core job is therefore covered by a state tool. The number of active LBCs was not found. Buyers are few and the state controls the data. Weak for a solo founder.

name: Excise Bill 2026 registration and stamp-stock desk for small beverage producers and stockists (local spirits, soft drinks, juice makers)
buyer: Small local distillers (akpeteshie, bitters), small soft-drink and beverage producers, and stockists of excisable goods
trigger: Excise Bill 2026, passed by Parliament 28 Jul 2026, repeals Acts 873 and 878; mandatory registration for manufacturers, importers and stockists, display of certificate, audits and stamp checks; sliding rate tied to local raw-material share; track-and-trace flagged in the 2026 mid-year review. Existing duty: stamps must be affixed before goods leave the factory or are sold (Act 873 s.4 registration).
duty: Excise Bill 2026 replaces Acts 873/878: mandatory registration of manufacturers, importers and stockists, stamps affixed before release, stock reconciliation, with audits and penalties; commencement unconfirmed
market: Not quantified; no register count found. Likely a few hundred to low thousands of registered producers and stockists, mostly informal.
competitor: GRA Excise Tax Stamp portal (ghanataxstamp.com) and GRA authenticator app; no private vendor found
reason: Duty is real: Excise Bill 2026 passed 28 Jul 2026, apparently assented 26 Aug 2026 (commencement date not found). It repeals Acts 873 and 878 and requires registration of manufacturers, importers and stockists, plus stamp affixing, with stamp provisions in clauses 46-69. Stamps have been enforced since 2018 via the GRA portal ghanataxstamp.com, which gives registered users access. Reconciliation of stamps to production and stock is required. No private product found, but the GRA portal likely covers ordering and reporting. Weak: tiny, informal akpeteshie producers, low willingness to pay, unclear periodic returns, no register count, and a state tool already in place. Fruit juice moved to 0% duty, which shrinks the market.

name: PVO re-registration and compliance service for small trusts, associations and community bodies
buyer: Small trusts, welfare associations, community groups and possibly church-run charities that seek outside funding or collect public contributions
trigger: Private Voluntary Organisations Amendment Act 2025 (Gazette 11 Apr 2025, General Notice 620): trusts lose exemption; register within 90 days of commencement or 30 days of starting operations; report material changes; refuse illegitimate donations. SI 97 and SI 98 of 2026 add risk-based supervision and AML/CFT expectations.
duty: PVO Amendment Act 2025 (enacted 11 Apr 2025): trusts, associations and universitas that pursue PVO objects and seek outside funds or collect public contributions must register within 90 days of commencement, or within 30 days of starting operations, whichever is later. Material changes (beneficial ownership, objectives, territorial scope) must be filed, with a civil penalty of USD 100 per day for up to 90 days. Running a non-compliant PVO carries a fine of up to level 12 and up to 2 years in prison. Further penalties of USD 100 per day apply for non-compliant donations and for having no bank account. SI 98 of 2026 (5 June 2026, FIU risk-based supervision): all PVOs must keep records of transactions and of donors and beneficiaries, keep registers of trustees, directors and key staff, run donor and beneficiary due diligence and sanctions screening, and report suspicious and threshold transactions. High-risk PVOs face more frequent reporting (frequency not stated) and must disclose beneficial ownership. Enforcement is graduated, up to revocation and prosecution. SI 97 of 2026 eases constitution rules and lowers the minimum committee to 5. Applications with no answer within 90 days become provisionally registered. I found no annual return frequency. The 2025 Act text on the religious-body exemption is unconfirmed: it appeared in the 2024 Bill guide, but I could not see it in the 2025 excerpt. The ICNL 2025 PDF returned 404.
market: Small. NANGO cites the Registrar: about 371 new registrations by March 2026 plus more than 400 existing entries, so about 700 organisations, which NANGO calls about 85% compliance. Any unregistered community trusts or groups are unquantified.
competitor: I found no PVO compliance software or SaaS. Existing help is free: NANGO's 'Talk to Your Regulator' platform and workshops, ICNL's practical guide, and law-firm commentary (Afriwise, Muvingi Mugadza). The state process is paper-based, going through district social development offices (forms PVO 1 and PVO 2). The ministry plans to train District Social Development Officers. General AML or sanctions-screening tools exist, but I did not check any local product.
reason: The duty is real and in force. The PVO Amendment Act 2025 says trusts must register within 90 days of commencement or 30 days of starting operations, and late material-change filings cost USD 100 per day. SI 98 (5 June 2026) requires all PVOs to keep records, keep registers, screen donors against sanctions and report suspicious transactions, with high-risk PVOs reporting more often. I found no software. But the market is tiny, about 700 PVOs on the register, and NANGO says about 85% have already complied. The registration wave has mostly passed. Buyers are donor-funded NGOs that get free NANGO and ICNL support, and the topic is politically sensitive. I found no annual-return frequency. Churches' religious-work exemption is unconfirmed in the 2025 text.

name: Cattle buying-agent and livestock trader movement-permit and stock-register kit
buyer: Cattle buying agents, small livestock traders and abattoir suppliers who move cattle between districts
trigger: Stock Theft Act duty to keep stock registers (dates, description, value); veterinary movement permit plus police clearance; branding under Animal Health (Livestock Identification) Regulations SI 35 of 2003; 2026 police operation (3,400+ arrests, failure to produce movement permits and registers).
duty: A veterinary movement permit is needed to move livestock between districts, and police clearance is common practice. The Stock Theft Prevention Act [Ch 9:18] requires butchers and buyers of skins or hides to keep a register of where stock and hides came from (names, addresses, brands). The penalty is a fine up to level 6 and/or up to 2 years in prison. A 2023 High Court judgment applied the register duty to butchers (S v Chidawaya). No register duty on cattle buying agents or traders was found in the Act text checked; the Criminal Law Code was not checked. Enforcement is current: a police operation launched in April 2026 reported 3,412 arrests, 2,997 of them for related offences such as failing to produce movement permits or keep stock registers.
market: The only figure found is an estimate from an EU-linked value-chain document tied to the 2014-2018 Livestock Development Program: about 1,160 traders or middlemen, 122 abattoirs and about 2,400 rural butchers. Another source counts 53 abattoirs. No official register of cattle buyers was found. Trading is largely informal, and willingness to pay looks low.
competitor: State: the DVS Digital Livestock Stock Card and portal (mobile and web apps; records ownership, movement clearance, transactions, health; training of vets under way before full rollout; reported June 2025). Private: E-Livestock Global, an RFID and blockchain traceability system built with Mastercard (2021). Permits themselves are issued in person by DVS and police, so third-party software can't issue them.
reason: The duties are real, but the core job is already taken by the state, and the register duty doesn't fall on these buyers. Veterinary movement permits and police clearance are issued in person by officials. The Directorate of Veterinary Services (DVS) is rolling out its own Digital Livestock Stock Card, with mobile and web apps, which records ownership, movement clearance and sale data (reported June 2025). E-Livestock Global, a private company, offers RFID traceability. In the Stock Theft Prevention Act text found (2016 consolidation), the register duty applies to butchers and buyers of skins or hides. That is the butcher side, already known idea K03, not cattle agents. The only count found is about 1,160 traders, mostly informal. A May 2026 police blitz made 2,997 arrests for related offences, including missing permits and registers.

name: Borehole registration and abstraction-permit filing service for households, farms and drillers
buyer: Borehole owners (households, small commercial farms, bottlers) and small drilling firms
trigger: Water Act [Ch 20:24] s34: drilling permit and registration with sub-catchment council, groundwater abstraction permit; SI 291 of 2020 fees; 2025 enforcement notices (US$205); drillers must supply construction, pumping test and yield data.
duty: Water Act [Chapter 20:24] (in force, as amended): s35(1) requires written authority from the catchment council before drilling or deepening a borehole, and an abstraction permit is needed to use the water. s37 lets a permit transfer when a property is sold. Penalties are under s118 and s24. Levies are paid to sub-catchment councils under the Water (Subcatchment Councils Rates) Regulations 2005, and a Harare letter cited SI 10 of 2012 / SI 47 of 2000 and quarterly levies. A court record cites s17A of SI 90 of 2013, which requires registration plus a valid permit. Enforcement: an Upper Gwayi notice in Sept 2024 threatened US$150 per unregistered borehole, and a Mbembesi notice in Feb 2025 charged US$205 in total. Masvingo and Insiza 2025 by-laws set fines of US$300 and US$2,000. Drillers must supply construction and pumping-test records. SI 291 of 2020 was not verified, and the permit renewal term was not found.
market: Figures conflict and are out of date. Harare: 1,848 registered private boreholes (PLOS/PMC cholera study, cited by Propzone), about 3,500 privately managed plus 235 run by the city (VOA, undated), and 28,000 registered (2021 SADC GMI review, as reported). Many boreholes were drilled without permits during the 2007-09 cholera period. There are probably tens of thousands nationally, but I found no register count. Most owners are households with little ability to pay.
competitor: My searches found no ZINWA or sub-catchment council online portal or app. Forms GW1 and GW4 are picked up from council offices. I found no specialist registration agent ("we register" search came back empty). Upper Manyame (uppermanyame.co.zw) and Nyagui (nyagui.co.zw) have websites, but I found no e-filing on them. ZINWA has a water-abstraction-agreement page (zinwa.co.zw) that I did not open. Drilling firms probably handle the paperwork informally. Botswana (BoreHive) and Zambia (ZamPass) have online systems, but those are other countries.
reason: The duty is real. Under the Water Act [Ch 20:24] s35 you need a sub-catchment council Authority to Drill (form GW1) and an abstraction permit (GW4). Councils enforce it: a Feb 2025 notice charged US$205 (US$100 penalty, US$55 application fee, US$50 registration fee), a 2024 notice threatened US$150, and Masvingo and Insiza have by-laws with fines. My searches found no online portal, app or registration agent. The process runs on paper at council offices. Weak points: registration is mostly a one-off. The levies recur, but sources disagree on whether they are paid quarterly or annually. Permit renewal terms were not confirmed, and fees differ between the many councils. Buyers have little willingness to pay, and drillers informally fill the role. I did not verify SI 291 of 2020. Market size is unclear: Harare figures range from 1,848 to about 3,500 to 28,000 registered boreholes.

name: Bureau de change licence and real-time transaction reporting tool
buyer: RBZ-authorised bureaux de change and limited-authority dealers (small family-run operators)
trigger: RBZ operational guidelines under SI 104 of 2015: prior authorisation, KYC/AML, real-time transaction reporting via the BDCTRS platform.
reason: The duty is real but the market is tiny and the state portal covers the core job. RBZ licensing is annual: licences expire 31 Dec and must be renewed by 31 Jan (policyvault ZWE127). Reporting runs through the RBZ-run BDCTRS, with applications at bdctrs.rbz.co.zw. A regalert summary dated 2025-01-01 mentions KYC/AML and penalties, but I could not open it (HTTP 429) and could not confirm that it replaces the 2019 guidelines. I found no third-party vendor and no licensed-BDC count after about 46 in 2019 (Herald), probably under 100 today. That is too few buyers, and they are hard to reach, so this is a weak solo-founder market. Penalty amounts were not found.

name: Vet-medicine general dealer (VMGD) permit and stock-record tool
buyer: Agro-vet shops and veterinary medicines general dealers
trigger: MCAZ guidelines for Veterinary Medicines General Dealers: permit, premises criteria, sale conditions; counterfeit veterinary drug raids with Council of Veterinary Surgeons.
reason: The MCAZ VMGD guidelines exist (permit, premises criteria, sale conditions, records, penalties under the Medicines and Allied Substances Control Act). I couldn't open the text because the FAOLEX/LEAP page returned 403. Current status and any permit renewal cycle or recurring returns are unconfirmed; one search summary said "Repealed: No" and another said repealed. No Zimbabwe-specific competitor was found, only generic agro-vet inventory tools (Bisafi, Zhulia in Ghana), which are out of scope as generic. Market size not found. The duty looks like a permit plus record-keeping, not a clear recurring filing. The buyer group is small, the willingness to pay is low, and the evidence on a recurring workflow is weak.

name: Vendor and small business licence-plus-tax-clearance wallet for council renewal
buyer: Street vendors and small shop traders registering with councils
trigger: Sept 2026 Harare order to relocate to designated sites and register; April 2026 National Informal Economy Formalisation Strategy; August 2026 proposal that councils and ZIMRA share registers and make tax compliance a licence-renewal condition (proposal only).
reason: Presumptive tax on informal traders is real, with registration for a BP Number. Council vendor registration and licensing are also real. The key trigger is not law. The August 2026 plan to make licence renewal depend on ZIMRA presumptive-tax compliance is only a Treasury proposal, with no instrument or start date. It is meant to run on a government integrated portal, which would be the state's own system and could displace a private wallet. I could not confirm the September 2026 Harare relocation order. Searches returned only 2017-2018 coverage. I found no private competitor, but past council collection of presumptive tax stalled amid vendor resistance. Buyers are offline, have low willingness to pay, and are hard to reach. I did no market count and checked no register. Score is low.

name: Car-dealer AML/KYC and sales-record kit for FIU designated-sector duties
buyer: Independent car dealerships and vehicle importers/resellers (many small, USD-cash)
trigger: Money Laundering and Proceeds of Crime Act 34 of 2013; June 2026 FIU designation of dealers: customer due diligence, suspicious transaction reports, regulatory data submission, record of every car sold
duty: FIU DG says car dealers are an FIU-supervised designated sector under the Money Laundering and Proceeds of Crime Act [Chapter 9:24]. Duties: CDD, suspicious transaction reports, regulatory data submission and risk assessments. Herald reports say the FIU fined 97 DNFBPs, including car dealers, for STR, CDD and risk-assessment failures, with maximum fines reported as US$20k or US$300k (conflicting). Not found: the designating instrument, its effective date, a compliance deadline, or whether there is a per-sale record or reporting frequency. The Herald/NewsDay article fetches returned 403, so details come from search summaries.
market: No register of car dealers exists. The FIU DG says no regulator registers them, so the count is unknown (not_reached). The NRA 2023-24 rated the sector highest risk and found 95% of sampled dealers import and trade only in USD cash. The 97 DNFBPs fined across all sectors gives only a weak hint at how many supervised entities there are.
competitor: The FIU goAML portal (goaml.fiu.co.zw, linked from fiu.co.zw) is the free state reporting channel. I could not open it, and how dealers register there is unverified. The only other vendors found were generic AML/KYC ones (an aiprise.com blog). South African dealer FICA tools exist, but none for Zimbabwe dealers. No Zimbabwe dealer-specific CDD or sales-record product was found.
killer: None found. The FIU's free goAML portal (goaml.fiu.co.zw) only covers filing reports, not CDD or keeping sales records.
reason: The duty is real but only confirmed through the press. FIU DG Chiperesa told the Zimbabwe Independent (about June 2026) that car dealerships are a designated sector supervised by the FIU, with duties of CDD, STRs and regulatory data submission. Herald reports say the FIU sent penalty letters to 97 DNFBPs, car dealers among them, for missing STRs, weak CDD and no risk assessments. That suggests dealers were covered before 2026. Reported fines conflict (US$20k vs US$300k). I did not find the designating instrument, its effective date or a deadline. Reporting appears to go through FIU goAML, a free state channel, but no dealer-specific CDD or record-keeping tool turned up. Buyers are cash-USD, informal, and there is no dealer register. That hurts reach and willingness to pay.
challenge_reason: I found nothing that kills the idea. No Zimbabwe dealer-specific CDD or sales-record product turned up, only foreign or generic AML tools (Dealertrack Canada, for example). FIU DG Chiperesa says dealers are now a designated, FIU-supervised sector with CDD, STR and data-submission duties, and the Herald reports car dealers among the 97 DNFBPs fined. Filing reports goes through the free goAML portal, but that portal is not a CDD or record-keeping tool. Four things weaken the case. The FIU guidelines page has June 2026 guidance for casinos, precious metals and stones, real estate and legal professions, but none for car dealers. No dealer register or registering body exists. The designating instrument, its start date and any deadline are still unverified. Dealers are informal, cash-USD sellers with no published count, so how many there are and whether they would pay is unproven.

name: Guest house, lodge and private-home ZTA registration, levy and VAT compliance pack
buyer: Guest houses, lodges, Airbnb hosts and private homes offering accommodation
trigger: Tourism Act Section 36 registration (deadline 28 February 2026, closures from 1 March 2026); 2% tourism levy on accommodation charges; VAT on accommodation reported at 15.5% from 1 January 2026; ZIMRA visits to guest houses and Airbnb
duty: Duty in force: registration and licensing with ZTA under Tourism Act s36 [Ch 14:20]. The ZTA notice set a 28 Feb 2026 deadline, and from 1 Mar 2026 inspections in all 10 provinces close unregistered facilities (fingaz reports 25 closed, businesstimes 30+). Scope covers accommodation including Airbnb and short-term rentals. Licences appear annual: fee caps are stated per year, e.g. US$150/yr for restaurants. I did not confirm accommodation-specific fee amounts or the renewal cycle. Expo private homes paid a US$50 temporary licence for Sanganai 2026. The 2% ZTA levy on revenue is cited in news and an MSU study, but I did not verify its current filing frequency, return form or portal. ZIMRA is running a compliance drive on lodges, guest houses and Airbnb, with returns via TaRMS and penalties, interest and prosecution for late filing. On VAT, secondary sources say 15.5% applies to tourism services from 1 Jan 2026 (2026 Budget / Finance Bill HB14 of 2025). ATTA mentions only activities and transfers, and I did not reach an official ZIMRA notice. The VAT threshold reportedly drops to US$25,000 (secondary source).
market: Not found. I found no published count of ZTA-registered accommodation, and Airbnb listing totals for Zimbabwe are unavailable. Closure figures by city (Gweru 9, Mutare 4, Harare 3, etc.) suggest a large informal base. Likely low thousands of guest houses and lodges plus short-let hosts, but this estimate is unverified.
competitor: I found no software that does ZTA registration, licence renewal or 2% levy returns. ZTA registration is manual (registration@ztazim.co.zw, offices, phone), and an April 2026 report says NetOne will digitise ZTA's inspectorate, which could become a future free state channel. For ZIMRA, the free ZIMRA POS app and virtual-fiscalisation API cover fiscal invoicing, TaRMS is the free filing portal, and Odoo ZW FDMS modules exist. Regional PMS products (ResRequest, Vistello, PAN Hospitality) do not document ZTA or ZIMRA compliance. I found no hotel PMS certified for ZIMRA FDMS.
killer: Partial, not a full kill: ZTA's free Online Registration System handles registration and renewals (tourismupdate, 2019), and NetOne is digitising ZTA licensing (2026). ZIMRA's free TaRMS and POS app cover VAT. The registration duty is annual and cheap.
reason: The duty is real. ZTA says registration under Tourism Act s36 (Ch 14:20) is mandatory, the deadline was 28 Feb 2026, and inspections with closures began 1 Mar 2026, with 25-30+ facilities shut. Licences are annual (restaurants are capped at US$150/yr). ZTA takes registration only by email, office visit or phone; I found no online portal. I found no PMS that handles the ZTA 2% levy, though ZIMRA offers a free virtual-fiscalisation POS app, and VAT returns go through TaRMS. Weak points: the registration deadline has passed, so the one-off rush is over. The levy's filing frequency is unverified. VAT on accommodation is reported only in secondary sources. The market is unquantified, and buyers are small, cash-poor and informal. Fit is better as a done-for-you service than SaaS.
challenge_reason: I found no product that fully kills this: no PMS or vendor handles ZTA registration plus the 2% levy remittance. Free state channels cover most of it, though. ZTA has had an Online Registration System for new registrations and renewals since 2019, and NetOne is digitising ZTA licensing from April 2026. ZIMRA offers TaRMS and a free POS/virtual fiscalisation route, and Odoo FDMS modules exist. Registration is annual and cheap (about US$200 for 1-3 star guest houses after the 50% fee cut), so there is little to automate. The levy (2% of revenue, remitted to ZTA) is the only recurring pain, but I could not confirm its filing frequency or portal. The buyers are small, often informal, and pay little. The Feb 2026 deadline has passed.

name: Private clinic / lab / consulting-room HPA registration and annual renewal service
buyer: Private clinics, medical labs, mobile clinics, group-practice consulting rooms, pharmacy premises, boutique and cosmetic clinics, rehab centres
trigger: Health Professions Act Chapter 27:19 Section 99; certificate valid one calendar year, renew by 1 January; separate registration per department; Material Change form on change of practitioner in charge; fees under SI 78 of 2017
reason: Duty is real: HPA page (fetched) says facility certificates last one calendar year, renew by 1 Jan, fees under SI 78 of 2017, and operating an unregistered facility is a Section 99 offence (fine, up to 2 years prison). HPA is building an online system with HITRAC, and the status is unclear. A UNDP-backed national health facility registry and the HPA registry tender are also in progress, which may replace any add-on tool. I found no Zimbabwe-specific renewal software. Market size is not found. The only count is dated: 32 private hospitals in 2015, and smaller clinics aren't counted. The workflow is a once-a-year form plus payment, so pain and willingness to pay are low. A small buyer pool and state digitisation make this weak as a standalone product.

name: Company and PBC re-registration done-for-you service (CIPZ portal)
buyer: Small companies, Private Business Corporations and sole-owner entities registered under the repealed Companies Act
trigger: SI 108 of 2025 (26 September 2025); deadline extended by SI 76 of 2026 to 20 April 2028; non-compliance means removal from the register and forfeiture of assets
reason: Duty is real: SI 108/2025 under COBE Act [Ch 24:31] requires entities registered under the repealed Companies Act (incl. PBCs) to re-register; SI 76/2026 moved the deadline from 20 Apr 2026 to 20 Apr 2028. Penalty is removal from register and possible asset forfeiture. It is a one-off duty, and the two-year extension removes urgency, so it is weak for a solo founder. Fees are reportedly USD50-300 (secondhand). The state CIPZ portal does the filing itself; lawyers and company secretaries are the likely manual competitors, but I found no named software or done-for-you vendor. No register count found. Market size, existing competitors and re-registration progress are not verified.

name: Non-profit compliance pack (CAIPO annual filing plus AML/CTF Commission annual NPO registration)
buyer: Churches, community groups, sports clubs, NGOs (volunteer treasurers/secretaries)
trigger: Annual AML/CTF Commission NPO registration renewal and CAIPO post-AGM filings; strike-off for lapses
duty: Annual AML/CTF Commission NPO registration, valid 12 months from first registration (Proceeds of Crime (Amendment) Act, effective 1 Jan 2019, per NOW Grenada). Fee EC$100-500. Failing to register is an offence: fine EC$5,000 plus EC$300 per day it continues. Also CAIPO filings within 15 days of the AGM (Companies Act amendment, 2014): annual report, financial statements, changes of directors. Non-filers are struck off under s.483 of the Companies Act (Jan 2023 gazette). These figures come from 2019-2023 news reports. I found no evidence of repeal, but I couldn't reach the primary law text or a 2026 source to confirm it is current.
market: 636 NPOs on the Ministry of Legal Affairs list (NOW Grenada, 2018). More than 600 per a later article. The claim cites over 1,000 NGOs/NPOs registered with CAIPO. These include churches, sports clubs, foundations, charities and political organisations. A very small market, and many have volunteer treasurers with little budget.
competitor: No private software or done-for-you NPO compliance service found for Grenada. The AML/CTF Commission's 2019 notice pointed to an online registration process at www.amlcommission.gd. That domain did not resolve in DNS today, so I couldn't check its current state. Search turned up no CAIPO Grenada e-filing portal. The 'CAIPO' portal results were all for Barbados's registry, a separate office. Accountants and lawyers probably handle this ad hoc (not verified).
reason: The duty looks real, but I couldn't confirm it from a primary source. NOW Grenada (2019-2023) reports that under the Proceeds of Crime (Amendment) Act, in force since 1 Jan 2019, NPOs register with the AML/CTF Commission every year (EC$100-500; failing to register is an offence, EC$5,000 plus EC$300/day). Separately, NGOs file reports with CAIPO within 15 days of their AGM, and CAIPO strikes off inactive ones. I found no repeal and no newer NPO Act, but no 2025-2026 source either. No private tool found. Since 2019 the Commission has offered online registration (amlcommission.gd, which did not resolve). The market is tiny (636 NPOs in 2018, about 1,000 at CAIPO), run by volunteers who pay little, with one or two simple filings a year. Commercially weak.
