name: Small-regulated-entity AML/CTF compliance pack (annual Commission registration, risk assessment, record-keeping, FIU reporting)
buyer: Used-car dealers, small law practices, real estate agents, money service businesses, small credit unions
trigger: Annual registration; STR duty; supervisory exams
reason: Duty is real. Under the Proceeds of Crime Act and the 2018/2019 amendments, DNFBPs (lawyers, accountants, real estate agents, car dealers, jewellers) and NPOs must register annually with the AML/CTF Commission via amlcommission.gd. Registration lasts 12 months and costs about EC$100-500 (2019 report). Penalty is EC$5,000 plus EC$300 per day (news reports). DNFBPs also file an annual PEP-related CDD compliance report. No Grenada-specific software found in 2 searches, but I did not open the commission site or the law text. The market is tiny: a few hundred entities, a small economy, and fees are low. Willingness to pay is weak, and the product is close to generic AML tooling or consultancy. Not checked: exact entity counts and the current fee schedule.

name: Tourism licence renewal and compliance pack for small operators (taxi drivers, guides, villas, guest houses, vendors)
buyer: Small villa/guest house owners, taxi and tour operators
trigger: Annual licence renewal and inspection; Airbnb MOU and pending short-term-rental registration law
reason: The duty is real. The GTA invites annual renewal each Aug-Sept under GTA Act 42 of 2013 and the Tourism and Beach Vending Act 18 of 2001. The covered categories are taxi drivers, tour operators, guides, car rental, watersports, hotels, villas, guest houses, apartments, cottages and named-site vendors. The core job is already served by a free state tool: the GTA's Pure Grenada tourism licensing portal, which accepts online renewal and has a QA help desk. The renewal page lists no penalties or required documents. The short-term-rental registration law is only described as "pending" in an old undated article, and I found no sign it was enacted. The market is small, with perhaps a few thousand operators. A paid add-on has little room, so the score is low. I ran no register count and no competitor-vendor search.

name: Household employer NIS registration and contributions for domestic workers
duty: NIS registration and monthly contributions by employers, including households if they employ; late penalty 10% surcharge plus 1% monthly interest
market: not found; no register or statistic of household employers located
competitor: NIS Grenada web portal my.nisgrenada.org (free state portal)
reason: The NIS duty is real. Employers must register, file monthly and pay a 10% surcharge plus 1% monthly interest if late. They file through the free NIS web portal my.nisgrenada.org. Contributions are due at month end with a 14-day grace period. NIS pages disagree on rates (13.5% vs 13%). I found no household-employer-specific rules, so a distinct household buyer group is unverified. Households with one maid are a tiny, low-pain, hard-to-reach segment. The free state portal already covers filing, and this is the same duty as K01 payroll. Market size not found, because no register or statistic was located. I ran only two searches and no fetches.

name: Owners' corporation compliance kit under the Building Management (Amendment) Ordinance 2024 (accounts, minutes within 28 days, high-value and large-scale maintenance tender records, document retention)
buyer: Owners' corporations (volunteer management committees) and the small property management firms and company secretaries that serve them; OC count unverified
trigger: Cap 344 amendments in force 13 Jul 2025
duty: Cap 344 as amended by Ord. 20 of 2024, in force 13 Jul 2025 (government press release and ISD TV announcement). OCs must follow procurement rules for high-value and large-scale maintenance. A large-scale project (average over HK$30,000 per flat) needs at least 5% of owners or 100 owners, whichever is fewer, voting in person. Financial statement, accounting document and meeting procedure rules are tightened, including minutes to owners within 28 days (seen in a search summary of the bill text; final wording not confirmed). Failing to keep certain documents is a criminal offence; fine amount not confirmed. Recurring: AGMs, annual accounts, and each procurement. Further amendments (five directions: voting thresholds, proxy transparency, declarations of interest, meeting procedures, authority powers) are only at consultation stage as of Aug 2026 district council papers. Not passed.
market: About 6,700 OCs covering about 12,000 of about 42,000 private buildings (DEVB press release, date not shown). Earlier figure: 7,294 OCs at Mar 2004. No 2025 HAD count found.
competitor: No HK product found that targets Cap 344 OC compliance (meetings, minutes, accounts, tender records). English results were US/Canada HOA tools (BuildingLink, Condo Control), which are not built for Cap 344. URA's Smart Tender scheme supplies a designated e-tender platform and independent tender monitoring for building repairs, so it partly covers the tender workflow for free or subsidised. HAD free templates and guidelines exist. Property management firms serving managed estates likely handle this in-house. Coverage of HK property-management software vendors was not exhaustively checked (search budget used up).
killer: None found. Partial overlaps: free HAD templates and the old Easy Count tool; URA Smart Tender for repair tenders (from the first check); property managers' in-house systems for managed estates (unverified).
reason: The duty is real and in force. The Building Management (Amendment) Ordinance 2024 (Ord. 20 of 2024) took effect on 13 Jul 2025. It requires a quorum of in-person votes for large-scale maintenance procurement (more than HK$30k per flat), tightens rules on accounts and meetings, and makes failure to keep certain documents a criminal offence. Fine levels not confirmed. A 2026 consultation on five more changes (proxies, declarations of interest, meeting procedures) is open but has not passed. My limited searches found no Cap 344 compliance product. The market is small: about 6,700 OCs (undated DEVB figure). Volunteer committees are unlikely to pay. Managed estates use the management firm's systems, and HAD templates are free. Possible overlap with K02.
challenge_reason: I ran 8 searches in Chinese and English and found no Hong Kong product that handles Cap 344 compliance for owners' corporations (OCs): meetings, minutes within 28 days, accounts, and tender records. Results were overseas homeowner-association tools (PayHOA, UpperBee, Condo Control, MRI), i-Account (a Malaysia-based billing tool), the HAD's old free "Easy Count" vote-counting tool, and HAD templates. Nothing found kills the idea. Weak points: buyers are volunteers; managed estates rely on property managers' in-house systems; the 2023 bill brief, not the enacted text, is the only source for the 28-day minutes rule; and the 13 Jul 2025 start date is unverified. Only about 47% of private buildings had OCs at end-2021, so the market is modest. A new Cap 344 review now proposes higher voting thresholds and clearer meeting procedures, which may add demand.

name: Employment-agency licence compliance and fee/receipt record kit for all licensed agencies (not only FDH)
buyer: About 1,971 non-FDH licensed employment agencies (3,888 total less 1,917 FDH) plus FDH agencies as add-on
trigger: Employment Ordinance Part XII; Code of Practice May 2024
reason: Duty is real: Employment Ordinance Part XII requires an agency licence (unlicensed operation up to HK$350,000 and 3 years). The Code of Practice (s.62A, in force since the 2018 amendment) requires written service agreements and receipts for all fees, with receipts kept for inspection. Commission is capped at 10% of the first month's wage. Breaches can lead to a warning or to licence revocation or refusal. I found no HK-specific agency compliance software. Results were only generic recruitment systems and Labour Department forms. But the duty is light: it is receipts and agreements, not periodic filings. About 2,000 non-FDH agencies are small, price-sensitive and already use paper or Excel. Willingness to pay is likely low, and this probably merges into K05. I could not fetch the LegCo paper (HTTP 503), so the 3,888 and 1,917 counts and the retention period are unverified, and I did not check for bespoke agency systems.

name: Food Safety Ordinance importer/distributor register and transaction-record kit
buyer: Registered food importers and distributors (count unverified), small wholesalers and manufacturers that supply other businesses
trigger: Cap 612
reason: Duty is real: Cap 612 requires importers/distributors to register (3-year cycle, fee about HK$195) and keep transaction records (3 months for perishables, 24 months for longer shelf life). Fines are up to HK$50,000 and 6 months for non-registration, and up to HK$10,000 and 3 months for record failures. Market: 12,738 registered traders at end-2013 (6,779 importers, 5,959 distributors), with no newer count found. Enforcement is light: 14 prosecutions in 2016. No format is prescribed, so invoices, ERP and POS already satisfy it. No dedicated software found, but this is probably because demand is weak. There is no deadline pressure and the willingness to pay is low. The duty and competitor searches rely on older sources, 2013-2017.

name: Mandatory Building Inspection/Window Inspection notice handling for small owners and OCs
buyer: Owners and OCs of about 9,200 targeted old buildings (of 20,900 aged 30+), via registered inspectors
trigger: Buildings Ordinance MBIS/MWIS
duty: Buildings Ordinance (Cap.123), Mandatory Building Inspection Scheme (MBIS) and Mandatory Window Inspection Scheme (MWIS), in force since June 2012. MBIS covers private buildings aged 30 or more, inspected every 10 years. MWIS covers buildings aged 10 or more, inspected every 5 years. Residential buildings of 3 storeys or less are exempt from both. BD sends an advance letter, then a statutory notice at least 6 months later. The OC/owners then have 3 months to appoint a registered inspector (RI), 6 months to inspect and 12 months to repair, plus 3 more months if there is no OC. MWIS gives 6 months for individual flats and 9 for common parts. Penalties: MBIS fine of HK$50,000 and 1 year in jail. MWIS fixed penalty of HK$1,500. Under s.40(1BD), a level-4 fine plus HK$2,000 per day. BD can do the works and recover the cost plus a surcharge of up to 20%. Fines in practice are low: an average of HK$2,200 over 3 years, which the Development Secretary has said should be raised (proposed amendment not confirmed). MWIS: about 98k of 240k notices from 2015-17 missed their deadline, so the pain is real.
market: BD's reply on the 2026-27 budget: about 20,900 private buildings are aged 30 or more, and about 9,200 have been selected for MBIS so far, leaving about 11,700 unselected. Audit report: as of end-2024, MWIS covered 27,168 buildings, with 13,461 selected and 723,219 notices issued since 2012. About 600 buildings a year are selected for MBIS (2024 report). The 2026 notice count was not reached.
competitor: No private Hong Kong SaaS for MBIS/MWIS notice handling was found (searched in Chinese for OC management apps and for MBIS one-stop/inspector-matching platforms; only generic or overseas HOA and property-management apps such as ec.Life came up). Free state-side alternatives already exist: the URA Building Rehabilitation Platform, the URA Smart Tender e-tender platform, the BD Care Your Building site and its lists of inspectors from professional bodies, and the HKHS/URA MBIS subsidy (this paid the full cost of the first inspection; whether it still runs in 2026 is unverified). Registered inspectors and property managers also handle the process for OCs as a service. The inspector-side buyer was not assessed.
reason: The duty is real and in force under Hong Kong's Buildings Ordinance. After a statutory notice, an owners' corporation (OC) must appoint a registered inspector within 3 months and finish inspection within 6 months. Repairs follow within 12 months, and buildings without an OC get 3 extra months. Penalties go up to HK$50,000 plus one year's jail and daily fines, and the Buildings Department can do the works itself with a surcharge of up to 20%. I found no private Hong Kong software for this, but free URA/BD tools cover most of the job: a cost reference, standard tender documents, Smart Tender and subsidy schemes. It is episodic, not recurring: each building is inspected every 10 years, with only about 600 buildings selected a year. Buyers are volunteer OCs who are hard to reach and pay little. Best folded into the wider OC-compliance candidate.

name: Private clinic licensing (Cap 633) application and Code of Practice compliance kit: incident management and reporting system, medical records, premises and staffing proof
buyer: Private medical and dental clinic operators, including those applying for full licences (813 applications by Jun 2026) and small practice clinics seeking exemption letters (3,026 requests)
trigger: Private Healthcare Facilities Ordinance (Cap 633). Clinic licensing in force 13 Oct 2025; provisional-licence window closed 13 Apr 2026; TVB (12 Jun 2026) reports that all private clinics must be licensed by end-2027. Unlicensed operation: fine up to HK$100,000 and 3 years in prison. Code of Practice for Clinics gazetted 23 May 2025 requires accurate medical records and a written incident management and reporting system. DH will inspect on site. Applications run through the DH e-Licensing System.
duty: Private Healthcare Facilities Ordinance (Cap 633). Licensing for clinics and small practice clinics has applied since 13 Oct 2025. The transitional window for pre-30 Nov 2018 clinics ran from 13 Oct 2025 to 13 Apr 2026, and all operators must now apply for a full licence. The Code of Practice for Clinics took effect 13 Oct 2025, and complying with it is a condition for issuing and renewing a licence. It requires a written incident management and reporting system, accurate medical records, patient identification and patient-rights policies, staff training and infection control. DH checks documents and inspects on site. Law-firm notes (Mondaq / Tanner De Witt) say a full licence lasts 5 years, which DH has not confirmed. Clinics run by up to 5 doctors or dentists can instead get a free exemption letter with no renewal. Unlicensed operation carries a fine of up to HK$100,000 and 3 years in prison (TVB), but DH said on 2 Apr 2026 that the date penalties take effect has not been announced. The 'all licensed by end-2027' deadline comes only from a TVB report. The licence fee was not found.
market: DH figures: 546 licence applications (193 of them provisional) and 2,712 exemption requests by 30 Mar 2026, with 26 licences and over 2,600 exemption letters issued. TVB, Jun 2026: 813 licence applications (118 approved) and 3,026 exemption requests (97% processed). Realistic buyers are the roughly 800 to 1,000 licensed (non-small-practice) clinics, many of them corporate or group operators. I found no official total of clinics in Hong Kong.
competitor: I found no software or consultancy aimed at Cap 633 clinic licensing or Code of Practice compliance. Searches in English and Chinese turned up only law-firm briefings (Mondaq/Tanner De Witt, Bird & Bird, Kennedys) and the official ORPHF materials, including the published Standards for Clinics. Not checked: whether clinic management system or EMR vendors (eHealth-subsidised CMS) already offer incident-reporting modules. They are well placed to add one.
killer: No killer product found. The weakness is market size and timing. Small practice clinics, about 70% of clinics, get a free exemption letter and appear to fall outside the Clinic Code. About 80% of clinics had already applied by June 2026, so the application-kit wave is mostly over.
reason: The duty is real. Cap 633 clinic licensing started on 13 Oct 2025, and licensed clinics must keep to the Code of Practice for Clinics (written incident management and reporting system, medical records, patient-rights policies, a chief medical executive with at least 4 years' registration). Searches in English and Chinese found no compliance product or consultancy. The case is weak on three points. (1) Small practice clinics (3,026 requests) get a free exemption letter that never needs renewing, and the Code is described as applying to licensees, so they mostly fall outside the market. (2) Only about 813 licence applicants, many of them corporate groups. (3) The licence runs 5 years, so the main event is one-off. DH said on 2 Apr 2026 that the start date for penalties is still not announced; the end-2027 deadline comes only from a TVB report. Clinic management system vendors could easily add this.
challenge_reason: I found no product or consultancy that does Cap 633 clinic compliance, so it is not refuted. But the market is much smaller than the claim implies. Most clinics are small practice clinics (5 or fewer doctors or dentists); about 70% are estimated to qualify. They take a free exemption letter instead of a licence, and the government rests their exemption on existing professional codes. The Clinic Code, with its incident system, binds licensees, so it is unconfirmed that it binds exempted clinics. The application wave is mostly over: about 80% of clinics had applied by June 2026, and the provisional window closed in April 2026. That leaves roughly 800 licensed clinics, often groups with their own admin staff. Their ongoing need, incident-reporting SOPs and records, is easy for clinic management system (CMS) vendors or templates to cover.

name: Security company compliance tracker: permit validity checks before each posting, 372-hour monthly and 12-hour daily caps, 14-day Police notification of staff changes, annual inspection document pack
buyer: Licensed security companies (about 1,300, per HKQF Jan 2024), especially small ones with a few dozen guards
trigger: Security and Guarding Services Ordinance (Cap 460). Licence conditions cap hours at 372 a month and normally 12 a day; the Authority's Common Omissions list flags posting staff without a valid permit, Type A permit holders working outside single-block private residential buildings, and failing to notify Police within 14 days. Revised regulations from 1 Jul 2023. Licence renewal and annual inspection require document packs.
duty: Cap 460, Security and Guarding Services Ordinance, plus the Security Personnel Permit conditions (Security Bureau / SGSIA). A permit holder must not work over 372 hours a month or, normally, over 12 hours a day. Before posting a guard, the company must check the permit is valid, for example through the SGSIA website. The company must tell Police Licensing in writing within 14 days of hiring or letting go of a guard. Permit renewal must be filed 3 to 6 months before expiry (s.15); late applications are refused and the guard must reapply from scratch. Type A and B holders aged 65 or over must give a medical certificate every 2 years. The licence is renewed and inspected each year. Breaches can lead to licence conditions or disciplinary action. I did not check specific penalty amounts or how often the rules are enforced.
market: About 1,300 licensed security companies with about 130,000 employees (HKQF, Jan 2024). I did not find a 2025 register count or a breakdown by firm size.
competitor: Workstem (Hong Kong HR suite for property management: rosters, multi-site attendance, 平安更 safety check-ins, patrol, payroll with allowances; I could not confirm that it checks the 372-hour cap or permit expiry because its page returned 403). Police app 警察牌照易 (e-permits and renewal reminders for the individual guard, free). Foreign guard-management tools with licence-expiry tracking: SecurityTime, Securecy, Guardhouse, OctopusPro. I found no Hong Kong-specific tool for permit, 372-hour and 14-day notification compliance.
killer: None confirmed. The closest threats are Workstem (Hong Kong property-management HR suite with rostering, attendance and payroll for security firms) and the info-tech.com.hk security payroll vendor. For both, it's unverified whether they enforce SPP validity or the 372-hour cap.
reason: The duty is real and in force under Hong Kong's Cap 460. Security Bureau guidance (2025) and the permit conditions say a permit holder may not work more than 372 hours a month or, normally, more than 12 hours a day. Firms must check that a permit is valid before posting a guard and tell Police Licensing within 14 days when they hire or let go of a guard. Permits must be renewed 3 to 6 months before they expire. I found no Hong Kong product built around these exact rules. Workstem, a Hong Kong HR, roster, attendance and patrol tool for property management, comes close and could add the rules. The Police app 警察牌照易 already reminds individual guards to renew permits. Foreign guard tools (SecurityTime, Securecy) track licence expiry. The market is small, about 1,300 firms, and the 372-hour rule is only one feature of a roster tool.
challenge_reason: Nothing I found kills it outright. Searches in Chinese and English turned up no Hong Kong product that checks permit validity or category against postings, enforces the 372-hour and 12-hour caps, or tracks the 14-day Police notice. The duties are confirmed in the permit conditions and licence conditions (ESCL). Three things keep it in doubt. (1) Workstem already sells Hong Kong security and property firms rostering, multi-site attendance, payroll with allowances and safety check-ins. Info-tech.com.hk also targets security-firm payroll. Adding the caps as rules would be easy for either, and I couldn't check either page (403). (2) The roughly 1,300 licences include Type III (alarm installers) that don't post guards, so the real market is smaller. I couldn't get a breakdown by type or size. (3) I found no enforcement statistics.

name: Chinese medicine retailer record pack: Schedule 1 toxic-herb dispensing register, transaction documents, online-sale site/premises mapping
buyer: Licensed Chinese herbal medicine retailers (4,634 licences in Mar 2015; current count not retrieved) and wholesalers (886 in 2015)
trigger: Chinese Medicine Ordinance (Cap 549) trader licensing. Retailer practice guide (4th revision, July 2025) section 6.2 requires Schedule 1 dispensing records; transaction documents kept at least 2 years per a LegCo paper; internet sales must be listed on the licence.
duty: Real and in force under the Chinese Medicine Ordinance (Cap 549) and its regulations. Schedule 1 herbs (31 toxic herbs) must be dispensed only against a registered CMP prescription. Licensed retailers must keep dispensing records, and the CMCHK retailer practice guide includes a reference format for the Schedule 1 dispensing record. Transaction documents must be kept at least 2 years from the transaction date. Internet sales are allowed only through websites named on the licence, supplied from the licensed premises. One search snippet calls the current guide the 5th revision (Oct 2025), not the claim's 4th revision (Jul 2025). I could not confirm which is right because the guide PDF did not render as text. The licence holder is liable for employees' breaches and faces disciplinary action. A 2007 LegCo reply cites a maximum level 6 fine and 2 years' jail for Ordinance offences. I did not confirm a specific penalty for the record-keeping breach. Whether electronic records are accepted: unverified.
market: According to the CMCHK/data.gov.hk CSV (updated 03/10/2026; the page shows the impossible date "31 September 2026"), there are 4,879 licensed Chinese herbal medicine retailers and 1,102 licensed wholesalers. Only 1,111 retailers provided dispensing services as at end of March 2026, per the May 2026 LegCo reply. Only those dispensing retailers carry the Schedule 1 prescription-dispensing record duty, so that is the realistic addressable market for this feature.
competitor: I found no HK product dedicated to the Schedule 1 dispensing register or herbal-shop compliance. The partial substitutes are: (1) the free paper reference format in the CMCHK practice guide; (2) CM clinic management systems with dispensing and retail modules (a 2009 OGCIO training deck lists 華佗, 長城 and 農本方; current features unverified); (3) generic HK retail POS (eRunlite, Cyberport-listed POS) without herb-specific compliance features; (4) LSCM's smart CM pharmacy dispensing R&D system, aimed at large dispensaries.
reason: The duty is real. Under Cap 549, licensed Chinese herbal medicine retailers must keep a dispensing record for the 31 Schedule 1 (toxic) herbs. These can only be dispensed against a registered CM practitioner's prescription. Transaction documents must be kept at least 2 years. I found no HK product built for this record. But the Council's guide already gives a free reference record format, and only 1,111 of 4,879 retailers dispense at all. Each shop dispenses Schedule 1 herbs in low volume. For the core job the competitor is the paper log, and CM clinic systems already have dispensing modules. Family shops are unlikely to pay much, and penalties seem to be mostly licence discipline. Best treated as a feature of a herbal-shop POS, not a standalone product.

name: LPG cylinder distributor customer-inspection and records tool (18-month periodic safety inspection schedule, gas contractor number on invoices, performance rating evidence)
buyer: Approved LPG cylinder distributors (small neighbourhood shops tied to a registered gas supply company)
trigger: Gas Safety Ordinance (Cap 51) and the LPG Distributor Code of Practice, 8th edition, June 2025. A distributor needs the gas supply company's written approval, must be a registered gas contractor, and must keep complete customer data to run an inspection every 18 months. Gold/silver/bronze Safety Performance Rating Scheme is audited by an independent firm and verified by EMSD.
duty: Duty confirmed in part. Cap 51 requires registered gas supply companies to monitor their LPG distributors (training, safety inspections, emergency response), according to a 1999 LegCo paper. EMSD's Code of Practice for cylinder LPG distributors (8th ed., June 2025) is the operating guidance. Per a search summary of its contents page, it covers a customer database (s.4.6), audits (s.4.11) and the safety rating scheme (ch.6). Each year independent auditors rate distributors on cylinder delivery, appliance safety checks, customer receipt records, staff training and gas safety operation records, and EMSD verifies the results (GIA, 30 Mar 2026). EMSD's public page tells householders to have a registered gas supply company or registered gas contractor inspect every 18 months. The distributor's own 18-month duty and record wording could not be read because the code PDFs are encrypted. The code is guidance plus supply-company contracts, so I found no direct statutory penalty on distributors.
market: 142 distributors under six registered gas supply companies took part in the 2025 rating (GIA, 30 Mar 2026): 67 gold, 26 silver, 49 bronze. In 2016 there were 184. The market is very small and shrinking.
competitor: No Hong Kong product for distributors was found in English or Chinese searches. The only results were overseas tools such as the SUPERGAS Care App (India) and SmartGasNet. A 2002 EMSD report says the code already focused on a computerised customer database. The LegCo paper says record keeping is a matter between the supply companies and their distributors, so the six supply companies probably dictate or provide the systems. Not verified.
reason: The duty is real. Under the Gas Safety Ordinance (Cap 51), registered gas supply companies must monitor their distributors. EMSD's Distributor Code of Practice (8th ed., June 2025) has sections on the customer database (4.6) and audits (4.11), and every distributor is audited each year for the rating scheme. But the market is tiny and shrinking: 142 distributors under six supply companies in 2025, down from 184 in 2016. A 1999 LegCo paper says customer records are a matter between each supply company and its distributors, so the supply company, not the shop, sets the system. I found no competitor product, but supply companies may run their own systems. I couldn't confirm the exact 18-month record wording because the PDFs are encrypted. Willingness to pay is likely low.

name: Money lender record and credit-data reporting kit
buyer: Licensed money lenders
trigger: Money Lenders Ordinance (Cap 163): licensing conditions revised from 4 Mar 2025, further guideline revision effective 1 Aug 2026; 2025 consultation (closed 22 Aug 2025) proposes mandatory credit-data sharing and an affordability check; a vendor page mentions a Credit Data Smart reporting date of June 2027 (unconfirmed).
duty: Money Lenders Ordinance Cap 163 licensing conditions; CDS reporting every 30 days from June 2027 (per law-firm summary)
market: About 2,110 licensed money lenders at end-2024 (down 7%); top 10 hold 79% of loans
competitor: Covenant Desk Lending (from HK$2,000/month); generic loan management systems; credit bureaus' own CDS interfaces
reason: Duty is real but small and mostly via licensing conditions. FSTB/CR conclusions (13 Mar 2026): phase 1 on 1 Aug 2026; phase 2 (Credit Data Smart reporting) rolls out June 2027, so the CDS duty is not yet in force. Law-firm summaries say unsecured personal lenders must report every 30 days (unconfirmed by the primary page). Market is about 2,110 licensees (end-2024), and the top 10 hold about 79% of lending. 36 lenders (about 64% of loan business) are already on CDS. Lender systems and HKMA/credit-bureau (TransUnion, Pingan OneConnect Credit) integrations serve the big players. Covenant Desk and generic loan systems exist. The long tail is small, with little willingness to pay and a single-regulation niche. The penalty is licence-condition breach, not a stated fine.

name: Estate agency AML/CDD record and self-assessment kit
buyer: Small licensed estate agency firms
trigger: EAA Practice Circular 23-01(CR) under AMLO s.7(1), effective 1 Jun 2023, Q&A updated 3 Oct 2025: CDD, record copies of ID, EAA risk-based supervision and self-assessment forms; consequences include inspections and disciplinary action.
reason: Duty is real: AMLO (Cap 615) in force since 1 Mar 2018. EAA Practice Circular 23-01(CR), effective 1 Jun 2023, requires CDD before the sale agreement, record keeping (5 years after the relationship ends), risk assessment, a compliance officer and an MLRO. Market: about 3,948 estate agency companies and 6,591 shops at 31 Dec 2025. No estate-agent-specific AML software found, only generic KYC vendors (Binderr, iCOMPASS), but searches were few. I did not verify the "self-assessment forms" detail, an EAA e-tool, or the penalty amounts. Score is low because the market is small (about 4k firms), the duty is mostly a one-off CDD checklist and file keeping per deal, and the generic KYC tools and an EAA template probably cover most of it. Willingness to pay is likely low.

name: Property management company licensing tracker (practitioner ratios, tier 1 CPD hours, licence renewals)
buyer: Licensed property management companies, especially small ones
trigger: Property Management Services Ordinance, licensing in force 1 Aug 2023; ratio of 1 licensed practitioner per 3,000 units (tier 1) or 1,500 (tier 2); tier 1 CPD 12 hours a year; penalty HK$500,000 and 2 years.
reason: The duty looks real: Cap 626 licensing, with practitioner ratios tied to unit counts. I could not confirm the 3,000/1,500 ratios, the 12-hour CPD figure, the renewal cycle or the penalty. The LegCo brief returned 503, and search snippets did not state them. The market is small: about 663 licensed companies at 31 Mar 2025 per one snippet, 800 per another, so the count conflicts. The regulator (PMSA) launched a free CPD-recording mobile app in 2022 for practitioners and keeps its own licensee register, which covers part of the core job. Few buyers, a free state tool and a small willingness to pay make this weak. Still-open checks: the PMSA licence validity period and any PMSA company-side portal.

name: TCSP licensee AML and licence-renewal tracker
buyer: Licensed TCSPs (6,840 at Jun 2022; many are small company-secretary firms)
trigger: AMLO Part 5 TCSP licensing: 3-year licence, Registry inspection of premises and records, AML pamphlets revised Mar and May 2025.
reason: Duty is real: AMLO Part 5 TCSP licensing (since 1 Mar 2018), with CR onsite inspections, an AML/CTF guideline (Mar 2025), and a CO and MLRO to be kept in post (7-day vacancy rule). Unlicensed operation carries up to HK$100k and 6 months. The register had 6,899 licensees at 31 Mar 2025. The 2024-25 CR report shows 1,130 inspections, 473 warning letters and 20 disciplinary actions. The Audit Commission found 568 late renewal applications in 5 years, which suggests a renewal reminder is a real but small pain. Competition: I found no TCSP-specific tracker, but the search was thin and the only named product was iCOMPASS, a KYC/AML platform. Generic company-secretarial and KYC vendors likely cover this, and many buyers are law or accounting firms with existing tools. Renewal is only every 3 years, so frequency is low and the MVP is mostly generic CDD and KYC. Low score.

name: Minor works registered contractor notice and completion tracker
buyer: Registered minor works contractors (individuals and small firms)
trigger: Buildings Ordinance Minor Works Control System: class I and II works need prior notice; completion certificate after works; registration expiry dates.
reason: The duty is real. Class I and II works need notice at least 7 days before start. All classes need a completion certificate (MW05) within 14 days. Registration renews every 3 years, and working after expiry has led to a $27,000 fine. But BD has a 2026 circular on a new Registration and Minor Works Management System (RMWMS, rmwms.bd.gov.hk). It offers online forms, an inbox, status tracking, iAM Smart signing and online payment. That is a free state tool covering the core job. BD also has a free MWCS app, and the older EFSS system. I found no private vendor. Registered contractor counts were last found for 2011: about 2,258 individuals, 228 companies and 1,853 provisional. These are old, so the market is small and the contractor is also the one required to file. Not checked: the registered contractor register today, and whether RMWMS has reminders.

name: Radiation Ordinance annual licence tracker for clinics, dental practices and vets using X-ray
buyer: Dental and medical clinics and vet practices holding irradiating-apparatus licences
trigger: Radiation Ordinance (Cap 303) s.7: licence needed to possess, use or store irradiating apparatus; annual renewal falls on the user.
reason: Duty is real: Cap 303 bars possessing or using irradiating apparatus without a licence, enforced by the DH Radiation Board and Radiation Health Division (offence carries fine and imprisonment). I could not confirm the current licence validity or renewal cycle, the current fee (the 2006 LegCo paper proposed $160 for a use licence), or current counts (only the 2003 figure of 8,365 licences and permits, all radiation types). I found no product or software for this, but I did not search specifically for vendors. The market looks small, with a few thousand clinics, dental practices and vets. Fees are low, and the paperwork is a periodic renewal handled through a DH form, so pain and willingness to pay are weak. Treat as a thin niche.

name: Annual FSI inspection tracker and FSD-letter response kit for owners' corporations, small building owners and property managers
buyer: Incorporated owners (OCs), small property management companies, owners of composite/domestic buildings and shop owners (also industrial buildings)
trigger: Fire Service (Installations and Equipment) Regulations Cap 95B reg 8: inspection by registered FSI contractor at least every 12 months, offence with max fine HK$50,000. FSD territory-wide special enforcement since July 2024, with warning letters, deadlines and prosecutions. 2026 consultation on amending Cap 95/95A/95B adds prior application for shutting down major FSIs (3 working days).
duty: Cap 95B reg 8 (HK law, in force): the owner has registered FSI contractors inspect installations at least once every 12 months. The contractor issues FS251 to the client and copies it to FSD within 14 days (FSD circular 2025/04). FSD prosecutes OCs; for example, 18 Eastern District buildings were convicted on 29 May 2025. The 2026 Cap 95 consultation (26 May to 25 June 2026) proposes an FSI responsible-persons regime, tougher penalties and fixed penalties, with a Bill due in LegCo in 2026. The detailed duties are not verified: the consultation PDFs could not be parsed.
market: Roughly 41-42k private buildings in total (DEVB, figure undated). About 19,300 private buildings had OCs in 2019, around 47%; by end-2021 the figure was still 47%, plus about 3,700 '三無大廈' (buildings with no OC, residents' organisation or management company). About 25k private buildings were 30+ years old in 2025. Several hundred small property-management companies are licensed under PMSA (count not verified here). The number of buildings fitted with FSI is not verified.
competitor: No dedicated owner/OC FSI tracker found in Chinese or English searches. The FS251 online submission channel is for contractors and has low uptake (2.7% in Q1 2024). Generic property-management apps (e管家/ec.Life, IWA 物業管理系統, CardApp platform) have no FSI annual-inspection reminder that I could find. Large managers such as Hong Yip and Kai Shing run their own in-house apps. HAD's 大廈管理中央平台 offers support briefings and is not a tracker. HKAPMC asked for an electronic or app channel for FSI shutdown applications, so FSD may build its own system (not confirmed). Not checked: whether contractors already send renewal reminders themselves (likely).
killer: None decisive. Main threat: FSD's enhanced FS251 e-submission system, live 18 May 2026 and mandatory from 1 July 2026 (Circular 4/2026). It gives FSD complete certificate data for automated expiry enforcement. No owner access or notification feature was found (unverified).
reason: The duty is real and enforced. FSD keeps sending advisory letters (571 in Q1 2024, 749 in Q3 2023) and has convicted OCs in batches: Kwun Tong (Nov 2024), Tsuen Wan (Feb 2025) and Eastern District (May 2025). The fire law reform consulted on in May-June 2026, after the Wang Fuk Court fire, adds an FSI responsible-persons regime and higher penalties, with a Bill due in 2026. Pain is rising. I found no owner-facing tracker. Generic HK property-management apps (e管家, IWA) show no FSI annual-inspection module. The core job is weak, though. It is one reminder a year, and contractors and property managers already prompt clients. Volunteer OCs are cost-sensitive. The new rules could also bring an FSD platform. Better as a module for small property managers.
challenge_reason: I found no product or free state tool that kills this. There is no owner-facing FSI tracker in Chinese or English. FSD's app only lets you verify registered contractors, and FSD's online FS251 system is for contractors only. Two facts weaken the claim, though. FSD Circular 4/2026 abolished paper FS251s from 1 July 2026, so all certificates are now e-filed with a QR check. The claim's '2.7% online uptake' figure is therefore out of date, and FSD now holds full expiry data it could use to automate reminders itself. Also, each building has one annual date, which the contractor usually manages, so the value of a tracker is thin. In demand's favour, the Wang Fuk Court fire led to a proposal making property managers statutory fire-safety gatekeepers. Big property managers have in-house systems, and volunteer OCs pay little.
